cards.headline: Anchoring: the first number sticks
lines: When we estimate, we start from the first number we saw and adjust too little.
In a classic study, a wheel rigged to stop on 10 or 65 pulled people's guesses toward that number.
Spot it: ask what you'd guess if you had never seen the first number.

visual.caption: Median guess, % of African UN members

cards.source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases', Science.

cards.headline: Spread practice out and you remember more
lines: Several short sessions beat one long cram for long-term memory.
Ebbinghaus measured this in the 1880s, and it has replicated in hundreds of studies since.
This feed uses it: questions you answer come back after growing gaps.
cards.source: Ebbinghaus, 'Memory' (1885); Cepeda et al. (2006), distributed-practice review, Psychological Bulletin.

cards.headline: Testing yourself is a way of learning
lines: Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it more than re-reading it.
Students who practised recall remembered more a week later than students who re-studied.
So the quizzes here aren't exams — they're the workout.

cards.headline: Confirmation bias
lines: We notice and remember evidence that fits what we already believe.
We also tend to ask questions that can only confirm an idea, not disprove it.
A useful habit: ask yourself, 'What would change my mind?'
cards.source: Nickerson (1998), 'Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises', Review of General Psychology.

cards.headline: Habits run on cues
lines: Actions repeated in a stable setting become automatic — the cue triggers them, not a decision.
That's why changing the cue (where, when, what's in sight) often works better than willpower.
cards.source: Wood & Neal (2007), 'A New Look at Habits and the Habit–Goal Interface', Psychological Review.

cards.question: A wheel showed a random number before people guessed an unrelated quantity. What happened?
options: Higher wheel numbers led to higher guesses
cards.why: That's anchoring: an irrelevant starting number still pulled people's estimates toward it.

cards.question: You have three hours to study for a test in two weeks. What usually works best for long-term memory?
options: Three 1-hour sessions spread over two weeks
Re-reading the notes three times in a row
cards.why: The spacing effect: the same time, spread out, produces more durable memory than cramming.

cards.question: Which study method has the strongest evidence for long-term retention?
cards.why: Practice testing rates among the best-supported techniques; highlighting and re-reading feel productive but help less.
cards.source: Dunlosky et al. (2013), 'Improving Students' Learning', Psychological Science in the Public Interest.

cards.question: The bystander effect says that in an emergency, a person is…
options: More likely to help when alone than in a crowd
More likely to help in a big crowd
Equally likely to help either way
cards.why: With others present, responsibility feels shared, so each person is less likely to act.
cards.source: Darley & Latané (1968), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

cards.question: People tend to like things more simply after seeing them repeatedly. This is called…
cards.why: Zajonc showed that familiarity alone can increase liking — one reason repetition works in advertising.
cards.source: Zajonc (1968), 'Attitudinal Effects of Mere Exposure', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

cards.headline: Working memory holds only a handful of things
cards.text: Miller's classic estimate was about seven items; later work suggests closer to four chunks. Grouping helps — that's why phone numbers are split into parts.

visual.caption: chunks held in mind at once

cards.source: Miller (1956), Psychological Review; Cowan (2001), Behavioral and Brain Sciences.

cards.headline: We remember the peak and the ending
cards.text: We judge an experience largely by its most intense moment and how it ended. In one study, people preferred a longer unpleasant experience that ended more gently.
cards.source: Kahneman et al. (1993), 'When More Pain Is Preferred to Less', Psychological Science.

cards.headline: Sleep helps lock in what you learned
cards.text: During sleep the brain replays and consolidates new memories. Studying and then sleeping tends to beat studying and staying up.
cards.source: Diekelmann & Born (2010), 'The Memory Function of Sleep', Nature Reviews Neuroscience.

cards.headline: The halo effect
cards.text: One good trait colours how we judge the rest. Thorndike found officers who rated a soldier highly on one quality tended to rate him highly on unrelated ones too.
cards.source: Thorndike (1920), 'A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings', Journal of Applied Psychology.

steps.headline: 1 · Encoding
lines: Attention decides what gets in — what you don't notice, you can't remember.
Linking new facts to things you already know makes them easier to encode.

steps.headline: 2 · Consolidation
lines: New memories are fragile at first.
Over hours, and during sleep, they are stabilised and tied to older knowledge.

steps.headline: 3 · Retrieval
lines: Each time you recall something, you strengthen the path back to it.
Recall also changes memories slightly: they're rebuilt, not replayed like a video.

steps.headline: 4 · Forgetting
lines: Forgetting is fast at first, then slows — Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve.
Spaced reviews flatten the curve. That's what review cards here are for.

visual.caption: Ebbinghaus: share of relearning effort saved

cards.headline: Psychology: the takeaways
points: The first number you see anchors your estimate.
We favour evidence that agrees with us.
Habits are triggered by cues — change the cue.
